prompt:
A code-review tool's test asserts:

`expect(review.comments[0].text).toBe("Consider adding a null check here.")`

The test fails intermittently — sometimes the first comment says "Add a null check before accessing this property" instead. Same finding, different phrasing. What should the assertion actually check?

options.text: Whether the comment text contains the substring "null check", plus that a comment exists at that line number
Add a retry so the test runs three times and passes if any attempt matches exactly
Lower the model's temperature to 0 so the wording becomes fixed
Remove the test — code review output can't be tested

hints: What does the test actually need to guarantee — that a specific sentence was produced, or that a specific finding was made?
A retry-until-match doesn't fix a wrong assertion, it just hides the intermittency in more attempts.
explanation: The finding — a missing null check, at a specific line — is the thing the tool is supposed to get right. The exact sentence describing it is not. Checking for the substring plus the line number verifies the finding survived rephrasing without requiring the model to be a parrot. Retrying until an exact match appears (option 2) doesn't fix anything — it just spends more API calls hoping to get lucky, and will eventually flake again. Temperature 0 (option 3) reduces variation but doesn't guarantee it away, which the next lesson covers directly — and even if it did, pinning the test to one specific phrasing is fragile the moment the prompt or model version changes. Removing the test (option 4) throws away real signal: whether a null-check finding gets produced at all is very much testable.

prompt:
A meeting-notes tool has this test, which someone weakened last month after it kept failing:

`expect(notes.summary.length).toBeGreaterThan(20);`

The original intent was to catch summaries that misrepresent what was decided in the meeting. Write a replacement assertion (in plain English, not code) that would actually catch that — and say what real bug in this tool the current version could not have caught.
hints: What has to be true of a correct meeting summary that has nothing to do with its length?
Think about action items specifically — they're the part of a meeting summary someone actually acts on.
The current check would pass for a summary of the wrong meeting entirely, as long as it was over 20 characters.
explanation:
A workable replacement: assert that every action item and owner name that appears in the transcript's decisions also appears in the summary, and that the summary introduces no owner name or decision that isn't traceable to the transcript. That's checkable without requiring identical wording, because it's checking facts (who owns what) rather than phrasing.

What the length check could never catch: a summary that's plenty long but attributes an action item to the wrong person, drops a decision entirely, or invents one that was only discussed and not agreed. All of those produce a string well over 20 characters. The length assertion isn't wrong the way exact-match is wrong — it's not testing anything adjacent to correctness at all, which is the more dangerous version of the same mistake, because it looks like a real check.

prompt: A receipt-scanning tool: reads an uploaded image, calls Claude with the image to extract vendor/amount/date, validates the extracted amount is a positive number, and writes an expense record. Sort each step by whether it's deterministic plumbing or the model's judgment call.

items.text: Checking the uploaded file is a valid image format before sending it anywhere
Deciding what the vendor name on a smudged receipt actually says
Validating the extracted amount parses as a positive number
Choosing which of two overlapping totals on the receipt is the real total
Writing the validated expense record to the database

hints: Ask whether the step's outcome depends on interpreting the receipt's content, or just on manipulating already-extracted data.
A step can call into the pipeline right after the model and still be fully deterministic, if what it does with the model's output is fixed logic.
explanation: The dividing line is interpretation. Validating file format, checking a number is positive, and writing to a database are all fixed logic applied to data — given the same input, they produce the same output every time, and you can test them with a hardcoded fixture standing in for what the model would have returned. Reading a smudged vendor name or picking the real total off a receipt with two numbers on it requires understanding the image's content, which is exactly the kind of judgment call that varies and needs a different testing approach — sampling real examples and checking accuracy, not asserting one correct string.

prompt: "Since we use temperature: 0 everywhere, it's safe to assert exact string equality on all of our model outputs, including full-paragraph summaries." True or false — justify in a way a teammate could act on.

config.statement: Temperature 0 makes exact-match assertions safe on any length of output.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and distinguishes short/constrained outputs from longer free text, not just a flat yes/no.

hints: Think about how many plausible token sequences exist for a one-word classification label versus a three-sentence summary.
Rare infrastructure-level variation matters more the longer and freer the output is, because there are more places it could tip a near-tied choice.
explanation: False, and the useful distinction is length and constraint, not just the temperature setting. On a short, constrained output — a classification label from a fixed set, a single extracted number — temperature 0 makes exact-match assertions reliable enough in practice, because there's little room for the output to vary. On a full-paragraph summary, even at temperature 0, there are many more token-by-token decision points, each one a small chance for batching-level nondeterminism to nudge a near-tied choice the other way, and normal model or infrastructure updates on the provider's side can shift wording even when nothing in your code changed. The safer default for longer free text is still to assert the properties that must hold, not the exact string.

prompt: A meeting-notes tool's action-item extractor is reported as "assigning action items to the wrong people." Before touching the prompt, what's the single fastest step to find out whether this is actually a model problem?

options.text: Print the model's raw response for the failing case and check whether the owner name is correct there, before it reaches any later processing
Add more examples to the prompt showing correct owner assignment
Switch to a more capable model and see if the problem goes away
Lower the temperature to make the model more consistent

hints: The lesson's whole point is: check whether the model's own output is correct before assuming it's the model.
If the raw response already has the right owner name and the final result doesn't, the bug is downstream.
explanation: Checking the raw response first is the fast, cheap diagnostic that either confirms or rules out the model in one step. If the raw response already names the correct owner and the final output doesn't, the bug is in whatever code runs between the API call and the final result — parsing, matching names to user IDs, formatting — and no amount of prompt engineering will fix it. The other three options all assume the model without checking, and are exactly the two-day detour this lesson opened with; they also cost real API calls and time before you even know if they're addressing the right problem.

prompt: You're adding a `formatCurrency(amount, currencyCode)` function to the expense categorizer, called after the model has already extracted a numeric amount. Describe the test you'd write for it: what's the input, is it a real model call or a fixture, and what does the assertion check?
hints: This function runs entirely after the model's job is done — does it need the model at all, even indirectly?
What's the smallest fixed input that would exercise a real edge case, like a value that needs rounding?
Exact-match is fine here — say why, in one sentence.
explanation: The input is a fixed, hardcoded number and currency code — no model call, no fixture derived from an API response, because by the time this function runs the model's job is entirely finished and its output has already been reduced to a plain number. A good test would include an edge case like `formatCurrency(9.005, 'USD')` to check rounding behavior, not just a clean value like `formatCurrency(10, 'USD')`. The assertion should be exact-match — `expect(...).toBe('$9.01')` or whatever the correct rounding is — because this is ordinary, fully deterministic formatting logic with a single correct answer, and there's no reason to loosen an assertion against code that has nothing non-deterministic anywhere near it.

prompt: "Any test that doesn't fail the same way every time is unreliable and should be retried automatically until it passes, with no further investigation." True or false?

config.statement: Any intermittently-failing test should be auto-retried with no further investigation.
config.rubric: A full answer distinguishes logging/pattern-checking from blanket retrying, not just a flat disagreement.

hints: What information does a blind retry-until-pass throw away that you'd need to tell a bug from noise?
The lesson isn't "never retry" — it's about what has to happen before or alongside a retry.
explanation: False. Retrying isn't the problem — some failures really are transient and retrying them is reasonable. The problem is retrying *with no logging and no pattern-checking*, which is what "no further investigation" means here. Before or alongside any retry, the failing attempt's actual output should be recorded, and failure rates should be tracked over time and across input categories. Without that, a real regression that only affects one category of input — like the refund-ticket example — looks identical in the CI log to ordinary network noise, and a blanket auto-retry policy will hide it indefinitely rather than surface it.

prompt: Match each failure pattern to what it most likely indicates.

pairs.left: Failures spread evenly across all input types at a low, steady rate
pairs.right: Flaky-by-design — likely infrastructure or network noise

pairs.left: Failures cluster on one input category and repeat the same wrong output
pairs.right: Flaky-by-bug — a real defect triggered by that category

pairs.left: Failures correlate with a known provider maintenance window
pairs.right: Flaky-by-design — external event, safe to retry

pairs.left: A test's failure rate has crept from 1-in-30 to 1-in-6 over three weeks with no logging to explain why
pairs.right: Unknown — the missing logs mean this can't be diagnosed without turning them on first

right: A test that should be deleted entirely

hints: The fourth pairing is the trap — the honest answer when there's no logging isn't a confident diagnosis either way, it's that you can't know yet.
Match based on whether the pattern points at the input's content or at something external to it.
explanation: The first three pairings follow the lesson's core distinction directly: even spread and correlation with a known external event both point at ordinary infrastructure noise, while clustering on a specific input category with a repeating wrong answer points at a real, content-triggered defect. The fourth is deliberately unresolvable as stated — a rising failure rate with no logging is itself the problem this lesson is about; you cannot tell whether it's a worsening bug or worsening infrastructure noise without first turning on the logging that was missing, which is exactly the fix from the first half of this lesson, not a diagnosis you can make from the rate alone.

prompt: A tool has two model-backed features: (1) suggesting a emoji to react to a Slack message, purely decorative, and (2) deciding whether to auto-close a support ticket as resolved with no human review. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Feature 2 deserves far more testing investment — it acts autonomously and a wrong closure means an unresolved customer issue looks solved
Both deserve equal testing since both are model-backed decisions
Feature 1 deserves more testing because emoji suggestions are shown to every user, so mistakes are more visible
Neither needs testing since both are subjective, low-precision tasks

hints: What happens, concretely, if each feature is wrong? Who notices, and what does it cost to undo?
Visibility (option 3) isn't the same thing as cost — a highly visible wrong emoji costs a shrug; an invisible wrong ticket closure costs an unresolved customer issue nobody's tracking anymore.
explanation: A wrong emoji suggestion is visible, mildly annoying, and costs nothing to ignore. A wrongly auto-closed ticket removes a real problem from anyone's queue while the customer's issue remains unsolved — it's autonomous, low-visibility once it happens, and expensive to discover and undo, since nobody's actively watching for tickets that shouldn't have closed. That combination is exactly the profile that should route the most testing effort, including the edge-case work from later modules in this phase, while the emoji feature is a reasonable candidate for minimal testing or none at all.

prompt: Name one feature from a real or hypothetical tool you're building or could build, and sort its pieces into: asserted deterministically, sampled and checked for a property, and deliberately untested-but-monitored. Say why the untested piece earns that status.
hints: The untested piece should be low-stakes and cheap to be wrong about, not just "the hard part to test."
Say what you'd monitor for in production as the substitute for a pre-ship test.
If nothing in your feature seems safe to leave untested, that's worth noticing too — it might mean the whole feature needs human review before any action, not more tests.
explanation: There's no single correct answer here — the exercise is graded on whether the three categories are genuinely distinguished and the untested piece has a real, stated reason rather than just being the piece that was hardest to write a test for. A strong answer names something concrete (e.g., a request-formatting function as deterministic, a categorization label as sampled-and-checked, and the exact wording of a low-stakes confirmation message as untested-but-monitored via user complaint volume) and explicitly connects the untested choice to low cost-of-being-wrong, not to convenience. A weaker answer treats "deliberately untested" as a place to dump anything inconvenient to test, which defeats the point of naming it as a real category.

prompt: A function that takes the model's raw JSON response and converts date strings from `MM/DD/YYYY` to ISO 8601 before storing them. What's the right testing approach?

options.text: A fixed set of input/output date pairs, exact-match assertions, no API call
Sample 20 real API responses and check that most dates converted correctly
Skip testing — date formatting is too trivial to matter
Retry the conversion three times and pass if any attempt is correct

hints: Given a known input string, is there more than one correct output?
Ask whether an API call needs to happen at all for this test.
explanation: Date-string conversion given a known input string is ordinary deterministic code with one correct answer per input — a fixed table of input/output pairs and exact-match assertions is both sufficient and the cheapest correct approach. Sampling real API responses (option 2) is the right technique for judgment calls, not for something with a single deterministic correct answer, and wastes real API calls testing something the model never influences. "Too trivial to matter" (option 3) is a common excuse for skipping cheap, high-value tests — date parsing bugs are a classic, boring, real source of production incidents. Retrying (option 4) makes no sense against deterministic code with no reason to vary.

prompt: "A component that calls the Claude API should always be tested with sampling and property checks, never with exact-match assertions." True or false?

config.statement: Any component that calls the Claude API should never use exact-match assertions.
config.rubric: A full answer names a case where exact-match is fine on model-adjacent code.

hints: What does line-of-code coverage actually measure?
Think about whether an assertion can be vacuous and still count as 'covered'.
explanation: False. Whether exact-match is appropriate depends on what's being tested, not on whether the API is involved anywhere in the pipeline. Code that builds the request sent to the API, or parses a fixed, hand-written stand-in for a response, is ordinary deterministic code and exact-match is correct for it — the API call itself doesn't need to happen in that test at all. Even short, tightly-constrained model outputs (a single classification label from a small fixed set) are often reliable enough for exact-match in practice. The rule from lesson one is specifically about free-text generative output, not about anything that happens to be adjacent to an API call.

prompt: Sort each testing decision into the module it best matches.

items.text: Using a fixed stand-in JSON object instead of a real API call in a unit test
Checking whether failures cluster on one input category before deciding to retry-and-ignore
Giving a refund-approval feature far more test coverage than a decorative emoji-suggestion feature
Logging a failing attempt's actual output before a retry discards it

hints: Match each item to the lesson whose diagnostic habit it demonstrates.
Two items belong to the same lesson — that's not an error.
explanation: The three categories map directly onto lessons three, four, and five: testing plumbing with fixed stand-ins is the diagnostic and construction technique from lesson three; checking failure clustering and preserving logs before retrying is the flaky-by-design-versus-bug distinction from lesson four; and allocating test depth by real-world cost of being wrong, rather than by how AI-involved something is, is lesson five's framework.

prompt: Match each symptom to its most likely cause.

pairs.left: Test passes with an assertion of `output.length > 0`
pairs.right: A weakened assertion that no longer checks anything meaningful

pairs.left: CSV rows have mismatched vendor/amount pairs despite correct model output
pairs.right: A bug in code downstream of the model, not the model itself

pairs.left: Test failures cluster on refund-tagged tickets with the same wrong category every time
pairs.right: A real, input-triggered defect (flaky-by-bug)

pairs.left: Test fails once in twenty runs with no pattern, correlating with a provider status-page incident
pairs.right: Ordinary infrastructure noise (flaky-by-design)

hints: Trace each symptom back to which lesson's diagnostic habit explains it.
Two pairs come from the same lesson — lesson four covers both flaky-by-design and flaky-by-bug.
explanation: Each pairing follows directly from a specific diagnostic habit taught in the module: a vacuous assertion is the failure mode from lesson one; a plumbing bug hiding downstream of an already-correct model response is lesson three's diagnosis; a clustered, repeating wrong answer is lesson four's flaky-by-bug signature; and a rate that correlates with a known external incident is lesson four's flaky-by-design signature.

prompt: Put these steps in the order you'd actually take when a bug report comes in for an AI-powered feature, following the module's diagnostic habit.

items: Check the model's raw response for the failing case
If the raw response is correct, look at the code between the API call and the final output
If the raw response is wrong, look at the prompt and the input it was given
Only after localizing the bug, decide whether it needs a plumbing fix or a prompt/judgment fix

hints: Check the model's own output before assuming anything about the prompt.
The branch you take depends on what step one finds.
explanation: Wait — note the correct grading sequence: checking the raw response comes first regardless of outcome, and the two branches (correct vs. wrong raw response) both follow from that single check, with the fix decision coming last. This ordering is exactly what would have saved two days on the CSV bug in lesson three: verify the model's output before assuming it, then branch based on what you find, and only commit to a fix category once the bug is actually localized.

prompt: A team wants "100% test coverage" for an AI-powered tool, measured the normal way (percentage of code lines executed by tests). Explain in 2-3 sentences why that metric can be fully satisfied while the tool still ships the kind of bug this module opened with — the invented refund policy.
hints: Coverage percentage counts executed lines, not meaningful assertions.
explanation: 100% line coverage means every line of code ran during some test — it says nothing about whether the *assertions* in those tests check anything meaningful. A test that calls the summarizer and asserts only `output.length > 0` executes every line of the summarization function, achieving full coverage of it, while catching literally nothing about whether the output is correct. Line coverage measures whether code ran, not whether it was checked, which is exactly the gap a vacuous assertion exploits.

prompt: A tool auto-drafts internal Slack status updates (low stakes, always visible to the whole team who'd notice if it were wrong) and separately auto-schedules calendar holds based on parsed meeting requests (moderate stakes, wrong holds silently block someone's real availability). Which needs the deeper test investment?

options.text: The calendar-hold feature — it's silent when wrong and costs someone real time
The Slack status feature — it's seen by more people
Equal investment — both are model-backed

hints: Compare not visibility but cost when each one is silently wrong.
explanation: Visibility to many people (Slack option) isn't the same as cost of being wrong — a visible bad status update gets noticed and shrugged off in seconds. A silently wrong calendar hold blocks real time on someone's schedule with no one flagging it until it causes a conflict, which is a higher, less-visible cost. This is the same blast-radius reasoning from lesson five's second half, applied to a new pair of features.

prompt: A team's 60-test suite makes a real API call in every test and runs on every push, roughly 25 pushes a day. What's the most accurate description of what this buys them over mocking the calls?

options.text: Nothing extra on most of those 60 tests — only tests specifically checking model judgment need a real call, and even those don't need one on every single push
Full confidence that the whole tool works correctly, which mocked tests can't provide
Faster feedback, since real calls are quicker than running a mock
Nothing — real API calls in tests should never be used

hints: Think about how many of those 60 tests are actually checking the model's judgment versus checking the plumbing around it.
The last lesson of this module argues real calls are sometimes worth it — so "never" is too strong a claim.
explanation: Most test suites are dominated by plumbing tests — request building, response parsing, error handling, downstream logic — none of which need the real model to verify correctly, per the plumbing/judgment split. Only tests specifically evaluating model judgment benefit from a real call, and even those don't need to run on every push at full frequency — this module's last lesson covers exactly how to decide. A real call is always slower than an in-memory mock (option 3 is backwards), and "full confidence" (option 2) overstates what any test — mocked or real — can offer, since a single real call is one sample, not a guarantee. "Never" (option 4) is also wrong, which is the point of this module's final lesson.

prompt: "Once a test mocks the API call, it can no longer catch any real bug — mocked tests are essentially decorative." True or false?

config.statement: A test that mocks the API call cannot catch any real bug.
config.rubric: A full answer names what a mocked test can still catch, and what it genuinely can't.

hints: The tagger's pass-through code, error handling, and request construction are all real code with real bugs possible in them — none of that requires the real model to test.
What's the one category of bug a mock genuinely can't catch?
explanation: False. A mocked test can catch a large and important category of real bugs: broken response parsing, a request built with the wrong parameters, downstream logic that mishandles a valid response shape, error handling that doesn't actually handle the error. All of that is ordinary code with real defects possible, and a mock lets you test it precisely and cheaply. What a mocked test genuinely cannot catch is whether the model's actual judgment is good on real inputs — that's not a gap in the mock, it's a different question that needs a different kind of test, covered later in this module and the last one.

prompt: Why is a fixture captured from a real API call generally more trustworthy than one hand-typed by a developer to match their mental model of the response?

options.text: A real captured response has the actual shape the API produces, including quirks and fields a hand-written guess would likely miss or get wrong
Hand-typed fixtures are always syntactically invalid JSON
A real captured response is always shorter and faster to write tests against
There's no real difference — both are equally trustworthy

hints: Think about what a developer might not know to include if they're guessing at the response shape from documentation alone.
The problem isn't length or validity — it's fidelity to what the real API actually sends.
explanation: A developer approximating a response shape from memory or documentation will tend to write a version that's cleaner and more predictable than reality — missing an optional field that's usually present, guessing at a nesting structure that's actually flatter or deeper, or omitting a quirk the real API has that nobody thought to mention in docs. A captured real response has none of that risk, because it's not a guess — it's what actually happened. Options 2 and 3 aren't real distinctions (hand-typed JSON can be perfectly valid, and length isn't the issue), and option 4 misses the entire point of this lesson.

prompt: Your team's fixture library has 12 fixtures, all captured 9 months ago, and nobody has touched them since. Propose a concrete practice that would have caught the stale-fixture bug from this lesson before it reached production, and say what would trigger it — not just "refresh fixtures sometimes."
hints: A trigger tied to a calendar date is weaker than one tied to an actual signal that something changed.
Is there a way to compare a fixture's shape against a real response automatically, without relying on someone remembering to do it?
explanation: A strong answer proposes a concrete, automatic trigger rather than a manual reminder: for example, a scheduled job (weekly or monthly) that makes one real API call per fixture scenario, diffs the real response's shape (field names and types, not exact values) against the saved fixture, and opens an alert or a PR if they've diverged — catching a shape change before it becomes a silent gap in coverage rather than relying on someone remembering to refresh fixtures on a calendar. A weaker answer just says "refresh fixtures periodically" without naming what would actually trigger the refresh or how drift would be detected, which is the same problem this lesson's scenario already demonstrates doesn't work reliably on its own.

prompt: Sort each scenario into whether a happy-path-only fixture library (captured only from successful calls) would or would not exercise it.

categories: Not exercised — needs a deliberate failure fixture

items.text: A well-formed categorization for a routine ticket
A rate-limit error during a traffic spike
items.category: Not exercised — needs a deliberate failure fixture

items.text: A second well-formed categorization for a different ticket type
A response that's valid JSON but missing an expected field
items.category: Not exercised — needs a deliberate failure fixture

items.text: The request timing out with no response at all
items.category: Not exercised — needs a deliberate failure fixture

hints: A happy-path fixture is, by definition, a captured successful response — ask whether each scenario matches that definition.
Two of these items are both successful responses, just for different inputs — that doesn't change which category they fall into.
explanation: Two items are ordinary successful responses (routine ticket, different ticket type) — exactly what a happy-path fixture library captures, no matter how many different successful examples it includes. The other three are failure modes: a rate limit, a malformed shape, and a timeout are all things a library built purely from successful calls has never seen, because by construction it only contains responses where the call went right. More examples of success don't add coverage of failure — that's the core point this lesson makes.

prompt: A tool sends one AI-generated email per day to a single internal recipient, reviewed by a human before sending. Compare this to the ticket-triage tool's continuous, unattended queue — which failure fixtures matter more here, and which matter less? Name at least one of each.
hints: Volume changes likelihood — one call a day makes some failures much less likely to ever occur.
A human reviewing before send changes what's expensive to mishandle.
Think about what happens if this one call fails outright versus what happens if the ticket queue's continuous calls fail.
explanation: A rate-limit fixture matters far less here than for the continuous queue — at one call a day, hitting a rate limit is unlikely, so building deep rate-limit handling is lower priority than for a high-volume tool. What matters more, relatively, is graceful handling of a clean failure (timeout, malformed response) since with only one call a day, a single unhandled crash means the entire day's task silently didn't happen, and nobody would necessarily notice until the recipient asks where their email is — unlike a queue where one failed ticket among thousands is a smaller, more contained problem. The human review step also changes the stakes of a wrong-but-not-crashed output: a subtly bad email gets caught before sending, so that failure mode matters less than it would for something unreviewed and autonomous.

prompt: A provider deprecates a response field a tool's parser has relied on for a year. The tool's mocked test suite is entirely green both before and after the deprecation ships in production. What does the continued green suite actually tell the team?

options.text: Nothing about the deprecation — the fixtures were captured before it happened and were never updated
That the deprecation doesn't affect this tool
That the parser correctly handles the field's absence
That the API provider made a mistake deprecating the field

hints: Ask what the fixtures actually contain, not what happened in the real world.
A green suite reflects what the fixtures represent, not what's currently true of the live API.
explanation: The suite tests against whatever the fixtures contain, and if the fixtures were captured before the deprecation, they still have the old field — the suite has literally never run against a response missing it. A green result here says nothing about real-world impact one way or the other; it's silent on the question because it never asked it. Whether the deprecation affects the tool, and whether the parser handles the field's absence gracefully, are both open questions the fixture-only suite cannot answer without a refresh.

prompt: "To keep fixtures honest, the drift-check job should automatically overwrite any fixture where the real API's response shape has changed, so the library is always current." True or false?

config.statement: A drift-check job should automatically overwrite fixtures whenever a shape difference is detected.
config.rubric: A full answer explains what should happen instead of automatic overwriting, not just that automatic overwriting is wrong.

hints: Automatic overwriting removes the one safeguard that would let a human catch a shape change worth investigating before it's silently absorbed.
What's the difference between the drift-check job's role and the everyday mocked suite's role?
explanation: False. Automatically overwriting a fixture the moment a diff appears defeats the purpose of the check — a shape difference could reflect a legitimate API update worth accommodating, or it could reflect something worth investigating (an unexpected field, a value that looks like an error being silently treated as normal data). The drift-check job's job is to surface the diff for a human to review and decide, then update the fixture deliberately — not to keep the fixture current at the cost of removing the one moment where a human notices something changed.

prompt: What question can a real API call in a test answer that a well-built mock structurally cannot?

options.text: Whether the live model's current judgment is still good on real inputs — a mock can only reflect judgment quality as of its capture date
Whether the request-building code correctly assembles the API payload
Whether the response parser handles a known JSON shape correctly
Whether the database write after tagging succeeds

hints: Three of these four are plumbing questions a fixed fixture answers just as well as a real call.
Which one is specifically about the model's current behavior, not about code?
explanation: Request-building, response-parsing, and database-write correctness are all plumbing questions that a well-captured fixture answers exactly as well as a live call would, at a fraction of the cost — that's the whole argument for mocking from the first half of this module. What a mock cannot answer is whether the model, as it exists right now, still produces good judgment on real inputs, because a mock's judgment quality is frozen at whatever the fixture captured, however long ago that was.

prompt: A solo developer maintains a small tool with no CI budget for scheduled jobs — just a manual `npm test` before each deploy. Adapt this lesson's advice: what would a reasonable, minimal version of a real-call quality check look like for them, given they can't run a separate scheduled job?
hints: The core principle — small, curated, property-checked, human-reviewed — doesn't require a scheduling system to apply.
What could replace 'on a schedule' when there's no automation for it?
explanation: The core principle transfers even without automation: keep a small, curated set of representative real inputs (even just 3-5) in a separate script, not run as part of the normal `npm test`, and run it manually before a deploy that touches anything prompt- or model-related — which serves the same purpose as a schedule, just triggered by judgment instead of a cron job. The check should still be property-based rather than exact-match, and the developer reviewing the output themselves before deploying is the human-review step, just without the formality of an alert system. What matters is preserving the separation (fast mocked suite for every run, a small deliberate real check before the moments that matter) rather than the specific mechanism used to trigger it.

prompt: A tool's mocked test suite has 15 tests, all built from a single fixture captured from one successful response. What's the biggest gap in this suite?

options.text: It has never exercised any failure mode, and all 15 tests may just be re-testing the same pass-through path in different words
15 tests is too many for a mocked suite
The fixture should have been hand-written instead of captured

hints: Count how many distinct scenarios one fixture, reused 15 times, can actually represent.
More tests against the same fixture isn't the same as more coverage.
explanation: A single success fixture reused across 15 tests likely means most of them are variations on the same happy path, with zero coverage of rate limits, malformed responses, refusals, or timeouts — the failure modes this module's third lesson focused on building deliberately. Test count isn't the problem (option 2 is backwards — more tests are fine if they cover different scenarios); a captured fixture is the right approach per lesson two, the problem is having only one.

prompt: "Since fixtures are captured from real responses, they never need to be updated once captured." True or false?

config.statement: A fixture captured from a real response never needs to be updated once captured.
config.rubric: A full answer names the drift risk, not just a flat disagreement.

hints: Think about whether the API itself is a fixed target or a moving one.
What would have to be true for a fixture to stay accurate forever?
explanation: False — this is the staleness trap from lesson two and lesson four. A fixture is a snapshot of the API's shape at capture time, and the real API can change (new fields, deprecated ones, updated model behavior) without any code change on the tool's side. An unrefreshed fixture can silently drift away from what the live API actually returns, and the mocked suite will stay green throughout, because it's only ever comparing against the frozen snapshot.

prompt: Match each testing decision to the lesson it best represents.

pairs.left: Replacing a live API call with an in-memory function that returns a fixed response
pairs.right: Why real calls in CI are slow, costly, flaky

pairs.left: Capturing an actual API response and saving it as a fixture rather than hand-typing one
pairs.right: Recording a real response and replaying it

pairs.left: Deliberately constructing a rate-limit-error fixture even though no real rate-limit event was captured
pairs.right: Mocking failure modes, not just the happy response

pairs.left: Running a monthly job that diffs fixtures against fresh real responses
pairs.right: Keeping a mock honest as the real API changes

hints: Match based on which specific problem each technique was introduced to solve.
Two pairs both involve mocking, but for different reasons — read carefully.
explanation: Each pairing traces to the specific problem its lesson introduced: the cost argument for mocking at all, the fidelity argument for capturing rather than guessing, the deliberate construction of failure fixtures nobody happened to capture live, and the scheduled drift-check that prevents a captured fixture from silently going stale.

prompt: Put these steps in the correct order for building a trustworthy mock from scratch for a new API-dependent function.

items: Make one real call against a representative input and save the full raw response
Build a replay function with the same signature that returns the saved fixture
Inject the replay function as a dependency rather than patching the module globally
Deliberately construct at least one failure-mode fixture for a likely failure given this tool's usage pattern
Add the fixture set to a scheduled drift-check that compares it against fresh real responses periodically

hints: The order should mirror how the module built up its argument, lesson by lesson.
Coverage of failure comes after the basic mock exists, not before.
explanation: This is the module's full arc in order: capture a real success case, wire it in cleanly via injection, deliberately add failure coverage a captured-only approach would miss, and finally add the ongoing safeguard that keeps the whole fixture set honest over time rather than letting it quietly go stale.

prompt: Sort each scenario into whether it calls for a mocked test, a real API call, or both.

categories: Both — mocked for speed, real for a scheduled check

items.text: Verifying the request-builder assembles the correct payload shape
Checking whether the live model's categorization quality has degraded on a curated set of real documents
The full CI suite that runs on every push
A monthly job checking both that fixtures still match reality and that judgment quality hasn't drifted
items.category: Both — mocked for speed, real for a scheduled check

hints: Ask what each scenario is actually trying to verify — code behavior or model judgment.
One item needs a combination, not a single choice.
explanation: Request-building is ordinary deterministic code, correctly tested with a mock. Judgment-quality checking is the one thing a mock structurally can't do, so it needs a real call. The everyday CI suite should stay mocked for speed and cost, per lesson one, while a periodic job combining drift-checking (lesson four) and quality-checking (lesson five) is exactly where both approaches belong together, each doing the part it's suited for.

prompt: A teammate proposes: "Let's just record every real API call our app makes in production and use those as our fixture library — way more realistic than hand-picking scenarios." What's one real advantage of this idea, and one real risk, based on this module?
hints: Think about what production traffic is mostly made of, versus what a fixture library needs to represent well.
Realism and deliberate coverage aren't automatically the same thing.
explanation: One real advantage: production-recorded responses would be maximally realistic and would likely surface edge cases nobody thought to construct deliberately, similar to the fidelity argument for capturing over hand-typing in lesson two. One real risk: without deliberate curation, the library could end up dominated by routine successful responses (since that's most of what production traffic looks like) and still under-represent rare-but-important failure modes like rate limits or malformed responses — the exact gap lesson three's deliberate-construction argument exists to close. A strong answer also notices this doesn't solve staleness on its own; a growing pile of old production captures still needs the drift-check from lesson four, or the newest ones become the only trustworthy ones over time.

prompt: A team wants to add a scheduled job to check judgment quality against real calls. Which design best matches this module's guidance?

options.text: 10-15 curated representative documents, checked for output properties, run monthly, with a human reviewing any quality drop
500 random production documents, checked for exact output match, run on every push
1 fixed document, checked for exact output match, run once and never again

hints: Check each design choice against a specific lesson's guidance — size, assertion type, frequency, and review step all matter separately.
explanation: The correct design combines every piece from lesson five: small and curated (not random and huge), property-based (not exact-match, since free-text judgment output varies), scheduled rather than on every push (to control cost), and routed to a human for review rather than a silent pass/fail. The other two options each get multiple pieces wrong — one is expensive and uses the wrong assertion type, the other is too narrow to catch anything beyond one specific case and never re-checks over time.

prompt: A bug report says a meeting-notes summarizer "missed an action item" last Tuesday. The engineer on call reruns this week's version of the tool against a transcript from a different, unrelated meeting, sees it correctly catches that meeting's action items, and closes the ticket as fixed. What's wrong with this?

options.text: Nothing was actually reproduced — a different transcript run through the current tool doesn't test the original failure at all
The engineer should have used a longer transcript
Closing tickets quickly is always the wrong call
The bug report itself was too vague to act on

hints: Ask specifically what input and configuration this test actually exercised versus what the original bug report was about.
Closing a ticket based on an unrelated success is different from closing it based on a reproduction of the actual failure.
explanation: The engineer tested a completely different transcript against the current version of the tool — that verifies nothing about last Tuesday's specific meeting, its specific transcript content, or the prompt and model version live at the time. The ticket may well still be open in every way that matters; the engineer has just gained unrelated evidence that a different case works. Speed (option 3) isn't the issue — reproducing correctly can be fast too. And while the report might be light on detail (option 4), that's a reason to go find the original transcript, not a reason the test performed was adequate.

prompt: You're investigating a bad output from two months ago. The original input is recoverable from logs, but the prompt template has been rewritten since, with no version history kept. Describe what you'd do — and what you'd say to whoever's waiting on the fix — given this gap.
hints: Is there a way to reconstruct an approximate old prompt version even without formal version history — git blame, deploy logs, old PR descriptions?
What should you tell the person waiting, given you can't get a perfect reproduction?
explanation: A reasonable approach: check whatever informal history exists — git history on the file even without a formal changelog, deployment timestamps that might bracket when the prompt changed, old PRs or commit messages — to reconstruct as close an approximation as possible, and clearly note the uncertainty rather than presenting the reconstruction as exact. The honest message to whoever's waiting states plainly what's missing: "We have the original input but not the exact prompt version from that day — here's our best reconstruction and what it shows, with that caveat attached." The wrong move is quietly testing against today's prompt and reporting it as if the original bug were confirmed fixed, since that's exactly the false-reproduction trap this lesson is about. This gap is also the strongest argument for building real prompt version logging going forward, which the next lessons in this module return to.

prompt: A translation tool starts producing awkward phrasing on inputs containing product names it used to handle fine. The prompt template is unchanged, the model version is unchanged, but the product catalog that gets looked up and inserted into the prompt was recently re-imported with different formatting. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: The context — the re-imported catalog data is now formatted differently when inserted into the prompt
The prompt — it must have changed even though the template file looks the same
The model — translation quality has degraded generally
There's no way to know without contacting the model provider

hints: Which of the three suspects has a confirmed, specific difference described in the scenario?
A re-imported catalog with different formatting is exactly the kind of context change that doesn't touch the prompt file or model config.
explanation: The catalog re-import is the one confirmed difference in the scenario, and it's exactly the shape of a context change — data assembled from an outside source (the product catalog) at request time, changed independently of the prompt template and model version, both of which are explicitly stated as unchanged. There's no evidence for a prompt change or a general model degradation, and reflexively assuming either (or reaching for the provider) skips the specific, already-visible difference sitting in the scenario.

prompt: Sort each item into whether it belongs to the prompt, the context, or the model suspect.

items.text: The fixed instruction text telling the model its role and output format
A user's uploaded document, inserted into the request
The specific model identifier string sent with the API call
Search results retrieved and included to ground the model's answer
A few-shot example baked into the template

hints: Ask whether each item is fixed template text or something pulled in from outside data at request time.
A few-shot example is part of the template even though it looks like content, not an instruction.
explanation: Fixed instruction text and baked-in few-shot examples are both part of the prompt template — they don't change per-request unless someone edits the template file. A user's uploaded document and retrieved search results are both assembled from outside sources at request time, making them context. The model identifier is its own separate category, since a version string change (or an unannounced provider-side update behind an unchanged string) is a different kind of cause from either of the other two.

prompt: Which of these, if missing from a log entry, would most directly prevent a genuine reproduction of a bad-output bug per lesson one's definition?

options.text: The exact prompt and context as actually assembled and sent for that request
The timestamp the request was logged at
The total number of requests processed that day
The name of the engineer who deployed the current version

hints: Go back to lesson one's list of what a genuine reproduction needs.
Which of these four items is actually on that list?
explanation: Lesson one established that a genuine reproduction needs the exact input, the exact prompt version, and the model version — the fully assembled prompt and context sent for that specific request is exactly that. A timestamp, a daily request count, and a deployer's name might be useful metadata for other purposes, but none of them let you reconstruct what was actually sent to the model for the failing request, which is the one piece of information reproduction genuinely depends on.

prompt: A team handles medical intake summaries — genuinely sensitive personal health information — and wants debuggable logs without creating a compliance problem. Propose a logging policy for them, applying this lesson's sampling-and-redaction idea to a case where the data itself is unusually sensitive.
hints: Sensitive data raises the bar on redaction specifically, more than it changes the sampling-rate logic.
Anomalous or error cases still need full detail to be debuggable — think about how to preserve that without preserving raw sensitive content.
explanation: A reasonable policy keeps the sampling and anomaly-always-logged structure from this lesson, but tightens what "full detail" means for sensitive fields specifically: redact or tokenize patient-identifying information before storage even for sampled and anomalous requests, while preserving the structural and non-identifying parts of the input and response needed to actually debug a categorization or summarization bug (document structure, which fields were extracted, confidence signals) without keeping raw protected health information sitting in a debug log. A stronger answer also notes that a shorter retention window is appropriate given the sensitivity, and that access to whatever full-detail logs do exist should itself be restricted and audited — sensitivity changes the bar for who can see the debug data, not just what gets stored in the first place.

prompt: "If a fix makes the originally reported bug's test case pass, it's ready to ship." True or false?

config.statement: A fix that makes the originally reported case pass is ready to ship.
config.rubric: A full answer explains what else needs checking before shipping, not just a flat disagreement.

hints: This module already established that a fix checked against one case is checked at sample size one.
What specifically should get checked in addition to the original case?
explanation: False. Passing the original reported case confirms the fix addresses that specific instance, but says nothing about whether the fix over-generalized in a way that breaks other, previously-fine cases — the exact failure this lesson opened with, where an absolute instruction fixed one missed null-check and then flagged several legitimate ones as risks. Before shipping, the fix should also be checked against a small set of deliberately-chosen near-neighbor cases that are legitimately fine, to confirm the fix didn't just move the problem somewhere else.

prompt: Put these steps in the right order for shipping a fix to a reported bad-output bug.

items: Reproduce the original failure exactly, per the requirements from lesson one
Isolate whether the cause is the prompt, the context, or the model, per lesson two
Write the fix targeting the isolated cause
Build a small set of near-neighbor cases the fix could plausibly over-generalize against
Confirm the fix passes both the original case and the near-neighbor set before shipping

hints: This sequence should combine the full arc of the module so far — reproduce, isolate, fix, then guard against over-correction before anything ships.
The near-neighbor set only makes sense to build once you know what the fix actually changed.
explanation: This is the module's full diagnostic arc in order: you can't isolate a cause (step 2) without a genuine reproduction (step 1) to test against; you can't target a fix (step 3) without knowing which of the three suspects is actually responsible; and the near-neighbor regression check (steps 4-5) only makes sense once the fix exists and you know specifically what kind of over-generalization it might introduce. Skipping straight to writing a fix without isolating the cause first is exactly the two-day-prompt-rewrite mistake from the previous module.

prompt: Why is running the original failing case only once, after a fix, insufficient confirmation — even setting aside the near-neighbor question entirely?

options.text: Because output variation means a single run passing could be luck rather than a reliably fixed behavior
Because the original case is never the right thing to test after a fix
Because a single run always takes too long to be worth doing
Because fixes should always be tested by someone other than the person who wrote them

hints: Think back to the earlier module's lesson on temperature and output variation.
The question is specifically about running the ORIGINAL case just once — not about whether to test it at all.
explanation: Even setting the near-neighbor question aside, a single run of the original case is one sample from a distribution that can vary — the earlier module's lesson on temperature established that even low-variation settings don't guarantee identical output every time. A fix could appear to work by chance on one run and fail on the next, or vice versa. Running it multiple times checks whether the fix reliably produces the correct behavior, not just whether it happened to once. The other options either misstate the lesson (the original case is exactly the right thing to test) or bring in unrelated process questions (peer review) not addressed by this specific point.

prompt: Walk through this module's full arc — reproduce, isolate, log, fix, confirm — applied to a bug you've encountered or can imagine in an AI-powered tool. Name one concrete action for each of the five steps.
hints: Each step should be a specific action, not a restatement of the step's name.
The 'log' step is about what you'd want captured, not what you'd do differently for this particular case in the moment.
There's no single right example — the point is applying all five steps concretely, not picking the perfect scenario.
explanation: There's no single correct scenario — this is graded on whether all five steps get a genuinely concrete, specific action rather than a restatement of the step's definition. A strong answer names an actual failure (e.g., a chatbot giving a wrong answer about a return policy), a specific reproduction action (pulling the exact conversation log and prompt version from that session), a specific isolation step (checking whether the return-policy document that gets retrieved into context had recently changed), a specific logging gap identified (the retrieved document wasn't being logged, only the final response), a specific fix (correcting the retrieval or re-indexing the document), and a specific confirmation (running the original conversation three times plus two adjacent policy questions that should still work). A weaker answer restates the five lesson titles without attaching them to any real specifics.

prompt: A team reports a bug "seems fixed" based on one successful run in a Slack thread, with no record of the exact input or prompt version used. What's the single biggest problem with this report?

options.text: There's no way to know if this was a genuine reproduction of the original bug or a different, similar-looking case
Slack threads are not an acceptable place to discuss bugs
The fix should have been tested by a different engineer

hints: Ask what specifically is missing from 'it seems fixed based on one run in Slack.'
Compare this to lesson one's definition of a genuine reproduction.
explanation: Without the exact input and prompt version captured, there's no way to verify this run actually tested the original failure rather than something that merely looks similar — the exact gap lesson one's whole first half is about. The venue (option 2) isn't the issue, and peer-review process (option 3) is a different, unaddressed concern that doesn't speak to whether a genuine reproduction happened.

prompt: "If the prompt template file hasn't been edited, the prompt can be ruled out as a cause." True or false?

config.statement: An unedited prompt template file always rules out the prompt as a cause.
config.rubric: A full answer explains why template logic can still produce different final text even with an unedited file.

hints: Template logic can still vary even when the template file's text is unchanged.
Think about what 'the prompt' really means once conditional logic is involved.
explanation: False, with a caveat worth naming: an unedited template file is real evidence, but template logic (variable insertion, conditional sections) can still produce a different final assembled prompt for different inputs even without the template file itself changing — which is closer to a context issue in this module's three-way split, but worth checking rather than assuming the template file check alone is sufficient. The safer check is diffing the actual final prompt text sent, not just checking whether the template file's git history shows an edit.

prompt: Match each scenario to the suspect (prompt, context, or model) it points to.

pairs.left: A retrieved document used for grounding was re-indexed with different content
pairs.right: Context

pairs.left: A provider updates what's served behind an unchanged model version string
pairs.right: Model

pairs.left: A template's conditional logic inserts different instructions depending on user tier
pairs.right: Prompt (or context, if the tier data itself is what changed)

pairs.left: A few-shot example baked directly into the template text was edited
pairs.right: Prompt

hints: Match based on where each change actually originates — the model, the retrieved/assembled data, or the fixed template.
One item is deliberately ambiguous — notice why.
explanation: Re-indexed retrieval content and provider-side model updates map cleanly to context and model respectively. The third item is genuinely worth sitting with — template logic is part of the prompt, but if what changed is the tier data feeding that logic rather than the logic itself, the real cause is context; the exercise credits recognizing that ambiguity rather than forcing a single clean answer. A directly edited few-shot example is unambiguously a prompt change, since it's fixed template text.

prompt: Sort each logging practice into whether it helps or doesn't help debug a bad-output bug after the fact.

items.text: Logging the fully assembled prompt and context as actually sent
Logging only the final categorization result and a timestamp
Logging the model version or request ID alongside the response
Logging the total daily request count

hints: Ask whether each logging practice would let you reconstruct the actual failing request later.
Aggregate counts and outcome-only logs answer different questions than debugging needs.
explanation: The items that help are exactly the pieces lesson one identified as necessary for reproduction and lesson three built the logging habit around: the full assembled request and the model version. Outcome-only logging and aggregate counts might serve other purposes (monitoring volume, say) but don't preserve what's needed to reconstruct a specific failing case later.

prompt: A near-neighbor regression set is being built for a fix to a customer-tone-checker that started incorrectly flagging enthusiastic-but-appropriate messages as rude. Put these in the order you'd build the set.

items: Include the original reported case — an enthusiastic message wrongly flagged as rude
Include a genuinely rude message that should still be correctly flagged
Include a different enthusiastic-but-appropriate message, to check the fix doesn't still misfire
Include a borderline sarcastic message, since tone-adjacent cases are where an over-broad fix is most likely to misfire

hints: Think about which case should come first to confirm the fix works at all, and which should come last to stress-test it hardest.
The genuinely rude message tests something different from the enthusiastic ones.
explanation: There's flexibility in the middle ordering, but the logical shape holds: start with the case that must be fixed, confirm the fix doesn't disturb what already worked (a genuinely rude message still correctly flagged), then specifically probe the near-neighbor space most likely to reveal over-correction — other enthusiastic messages, and the more adversarial borderline case last, since it's the hardest and most revealing test of whether the fix over-generalized.

prompt: A fix ships after passing the original case three times and two near-neighbor cases. A month later, a genuinely new failure mode appears — nothing like the original bug or the near-neighbors tested. Did the confirmation process in this module fail? Explain in 2-3 sentences.
hints: A bounded confirmation process was never meant to catch every conceivable future bug — ask what it was actually meant to verify.
explanation: No — confirmation, as this module defines it, was never meant to guarantee no future bug of any kind, only to verify the specific fix against the specific case it addressed and its likely blast radius. A genuinely new, unrelated failure mode is a different bug entirely, not evidence the confirmation process for the first one was inadequate — expecting any bounded confirmation process to catch every possible future failure would push back toward the unsustainable exhaustive-testing trap the earlier module already argued against. The right response to the new bug is running this same module's process again, from reproduction, on the new failure — not concluding the original fix's confirmation was insufficient.

prompt: Which best describes why 'reproduce before you fix' and 'confirm with more than one example' are really the same discipline applied at two different points?

options.text: Both refuse to trust a single observation — one bad run isn't proof of a bug, and one good run isn't proof of a fix
They're unrelated — one is about debugging, the other about testing
Both exist only because AI output is expensive to generate

hints: Look for the shared underlying principle about single data points, not the surface difference between debugging and testing.
explanation: Reproducing before fixing refuses to act on an unverified bug report; confirming with more than one example refuses to declare victory on an unverified fix. Both apply the same underlying discipline — don't trust a single data point in a system with real output variation — just at the start and the end of the same process, rather than being separate concerns. Cost (option 3) is a real consideration elsewhere in the phase but isn't what connects these two specific practices.

prompt: A teammate says: "We don't have time to build a near-neighbor regression set for every single bug fix — most of our fixes are one-line prompt tweaks." Is a near-neighbor set always worth building, regardless of how small the fix is? Explain your reasoning in 2-3 sentences.
hints: Line count and blast radius aren't the same measurement — a tiny diff can still touch a high-stakes, absolute instruction.
explanation: Not automatically — the module's own reasoning about matching effort to stakes and likelihood applies here too. A one-line tweak to a narrow, low-stakes instruction (say, adjusting the wording of a greeting) carries little risk of the kind of broad over-correction this module's lesson four describes, so a full near-neighbor set may not earn its cost. A one-line tweak that changes an absolute instruction governing a high-stakes judgment call (like the null-pointer risk flag, or anything gating an autonomous action) is exactly the shape most likely to over-generalize, regardless of how small the diff looks, and deserves the check even at one line. The size of the code change and the size of its potential blast radius are not the same thing.

prompt: A team tested their invoice-parsing tool with 200 real invoices from their own vendor list, all well-formatted PDFs under 5 pages. What's the biggest blind spot this test set has, given this lesson?

options.text: It never includes an empty, oversized, or malformed file, since 200 realistic invoices are still all realistic and well-formed
200 invoices isn't a large enough sample size
The invoices should have come from a randomized set of vendors instead of the known vendor list

hints: The blind spot isn't about how many examples there are — it's about what category of input none of them represent.
A larger set of well-formed invoices still doesn't include a single malformed or empty one.
explanation: Sample size (option 2) isn't the issue — 2,000 well-formatted invoices would have the exact same blind spot as 200, because the missing category isn't 'more realistic examples,' it's 'any example that isn't realistic and well-formed.' Randomizing vendors (option 3) might add variety within the well-formed category but still wouldn't include an empty file, an oversized one, or a corrupted upload — the specific gap this lesson identifies.

prompt: "When a tool can't fully process an oversized input, silently processing just the part that fits is better than an error message, because it still gives the user something useful." True or false?

config.statement: Silently processing only part of an oversized input is better than an error message.
config.rubric: A full answer explains why an invisible partial result is worse than a visible failure, not just that it's suboptimal.

hints: Think about what the user assumes when they receive output with no warning attached.
Compare what a user does differently after a clear error versus after an unmarked partial result.
explanation: False. A silent partial result is more dangerous than a clear error, not less, because the user has no way to know it's incomplete — they'll reasonably treat a confident-looking summary as covering the whole document, which is exactly the failure mode that matters most for anything with real consequences (a contract, a legal document, financial terms). A clear error, or a visibly-labeled partial result with an offer to continue, at least lets the user know something didn't fully happen and choose what to do next. 'Gives the user something' isn't the same as giving them something they can trust.

prompt: A team says their test set is thorough because it includes 500 different resumes from 500 different real candidates. What question would reveal whether this test set actually covers what this lesson is about?

options.text: How many of those 500 use a non-English language, a right-to-left script, or a non-Western date or name convention?
How many of the 500 candidates were actually hired?
Whether the 500 resumes were collected over more than one year

hints: 500 examples of the same format convention is still one convention, no matter how many candidates they represent.
The relevant axis here is format and convention diversity, not sample size or recency.
explanation: The number of distinct candidates (500) says nothing about format diversity — all 500 could still be English-language, Western-name-order, month-first-date resumes, which is exactly the narrow-but-large trap this lesson describes. Whether candidates were hired or how recent the resumes are doesn't bear on format coverage at all. The only question that actually reveals the gap is whether the set includes resumes from outside the tested convention.

prompt: Of the four format-assumption failures in this lesson's evidence-stack drill (name order, address order, phone format, currency separator), the currency one was singled out as especially dangerous. Explain why, in terms of what a user or reviewer would actually see when it goes wrong.
hints: Compare what each of the four failures looks like on the screen when it happens — visible error, obviously wrong result, or a plausible-looking wrong result?
Think specifically about what happens to the numeric value when a decimal separator gets misread.
explanation: A misread name order or address order tends to produce a result that's visibly odd — a name in an unexpected order, an address that looks garbled — which a human reviewing the output has a real chance of noticing. A misread currency separator does something different: "1.234,56" misread as "1,234.56" doesn't look garbled at all, it looks like a perfectly ordinary number — it's just off by a factor of roughly a thousand, in either direction depending on which way the misreading goes. That combination — looks completely normal, is silently and substantially wrong — is what makes it more dangerous than the other three failures, which at least tend to announce themselves by looking obviously off.

prompt: A structured-data extraction tool returns a JSON object that perfectly matches its expected schema — every field present, every type correct — but has swapped the values of two fields (the phone number appears in the email field's slot and vice versa, both as plausible-looking strings in their own right... actually, more precisely: both fields contain validly-typed strings, just the wrong ones). What kind of check would catch this?

options.text: A known-answer case checking that specific field values match specific expected values, not just that the shape is correct
A stricter JSON schema with more required fields
Re-running schema validation twice to be sure

hints: Schema validation checks shape and type — a swapped-but-validly-typed value passes that check every time.
What's the one thing that could actually tell the phone number field contains an email address instead?
explanation: A schema check confirms every field exists and has the right type, which two swapped, correctly-typed string values satisfy perfectly — no schema, however strict, can catch a value being logically in the wrong field if both fields are the same type. Running the same schema check again (option 3) adds nothing new. Only a known-answer test case — one where you know in advance which specific values belong in which specific fields — can catch this, by asserting the actual expected value against each field rather than just its shape.

prompt: A teammate proposes: "Let's just have the model double-check its own output before returning it — ask it 'is this correct?' as a second step." Does this solve the valid-but-wrong problem from this lesson? Explain the real limitation.
hints: Think about what's actually verifying the answer in this proposal — is it an independent source of truth, or the same source that produced the possibly-wrong answer?
Compare this to the known-answer case approach — what does a known-answer case have that a self-check doesn't?
explanation: This doesn't fully solve the problem, because the model checking its own output is not an independent source of truth — if the same reasoning that produced the off-by-one error or the wrong-but-valid category is asked to evaluate that same output, there's no guarantee it will catch a mistake it just made, especially if the mistake stems from a systematic misunderstanding rather than a random slip. A self-check step can genuinely help catch some errors and is a reasonable additional layer, but it's not a substitute for a known-answer case with a verifiable expected value from an independent source (a human-verified correct answer, a deterministic calculation) — which is the one thing that can actually confirm correctness rather than just get a second opinion from the same fallible source.

prompt: Why is structurally separating system instructions from user content (as distinct API fields) a stronger defense than trying to detect and block phrases like "ignore your previous instructions"?

options.text: Phrase-blocking is a losing game against endless rephrasing, while structural separation removes the mechanism the attack depends on regardless of wording
Phrase-blocking is illegal in most jurisdictions
Structural separation makes the tool faster

hints: Think about how many different ways someone could phrase the same underlying attempt.
One of these defenses depends on wording; the other doesn't.
explanation: An attacker can rephrase "ignore your previous instructions" in effectively unlimited ways, which makes any list of blocked phrases a permanent, losing game of catch-up. Structural separation works differently — it doesn't depend on recognizing any particular wording at all, because the model has been told, architecturally, that content in the user channel is data regardless of what it says. That's a fundamentally more durable defense against the same underlying attack, independent of how it's phrased. Speed and legality aren't relevant considerations here.

prompt: Match each adversarial technique to the layer of defense that actually addresses it.

pairs.left: A user message reading "ignore your previous instructions"
pairs.right: System/user channel separation

pairs.left: Hidden white-on-white text embedded inside an uploaded document
pairs.right: Content-level scanning of extracted document text

pairs.left: Keyword-stuffing inside a résumé aimed at gaming a scoring rubric
pairs.right: Content-level scanning of extracted document text

pairs.left: A search-result snippet accidentally pasted into a chat that reads like a system instruction
pairs.right: System/user channel separation

hints: Ask whether each technique is arriving as a user message impersonating an instruction, or as content buried inside something the tool is meant to read.
Two of these are really the same category as each other, just with different intent behind them.
explanation: The first and fourth items are both instruction-shaped text arriving through the user-message channel — one deliberate, one likely accidental — and both are addressed by the same structural fix: treating user-channel content as data, never instructions. The second and third are a different category entirely: adversarial content hidden inside a document the tool is supposed to read and evaluate, which channel separation doesn't touch at all, since the document's content is legitimately being processed as data — it just happens to contain a manipulation attempt within that data.

prompt: A team's edge-case checklist is comprehensive and well-written but lives in a document only the original author knows the location of. What's the most direct fix, based on this lesson?

options.text: Move a short version of it into a workflow point the whole team already passes through, like the PR template
Make the document even more comprehensive so it's worth the effort of finding
Schedule a training session to teach the team where the document lives

hints: The problem is location and timing, not content quality or awareness at a single point in time.
A training session is itself a one-time event, similar to the one-time email this lesson already ruled out.
explanation: The core problem is that the checklist lives outside the workflow, which means it depends on someone remembering to seek it out — making it longer (option 2) makes that problem worse, not better, since a longer document is even less likely to get read once found. A training session (option 3) has the same one-time-event weakness as the email in this lesson's opening scenario — it fades from memory the same way, and doesn't help anyone who joins later. Embedding a short version directly in a workflow checkpoint everyone already passes through is the only option that removes the 'remember it exists' requirement entirely.

prompt: For a solo developer with no PR review process and no team to embed a checklist for, what would the equivalent of 'build it into the workflow' look like? Propose a concrete mechanism.
hints: The core principle — a checkpoint every relevant change already passes through — doesn't require a team or a PR process to apply.
What does a solo developer's deploy process already include that a short checklist could attach to?
explanation: The underlying principle transfers even without a team: find whatever step already exists right before something ships — a deploy script, a pre-commit hook, a manual checklist in the terminal before running `deploy`, or even a short comment block at the top of the deploy script itself — and attach the five-question version there, so it's seen at the actual moment of shipping rather than living in a separate notes file that has to be remembered and opened separately. A pre-commit or pre-deploy hook that prints the five questions (even without blocking anything) achieves the same 'encountered at the point of decision' property a PR template achieves for a team, just automated instead of social.

prompt: A meeting-transcription summarizer is tested with dozens of real English-language meeting recordings of varying lengths, all clearly recorded with good audio quality. What edge-case category is most likely still untested here?

options.text: Format and convention diversity — non-English audio, heavy accents, or multiple overlapping speakers were never included
Empty input, since some of the recordings are surely very short
Adversarial input, since audio can't be adversarial

hints: Varying lengths of the same kind of audio still tests within one convention.
Ask what dimension of variety is actually missing, not how much volume of testing exists.
explanation: Varying lengths of clear, English-language audio still tests within one language and one audio-quality convention — the gap is format diversity: non-English speech, heavy accents, or overlapping speakers, none of which 'varying lengths of good English audio' would ever exercise. Short recordings aren't the same as empty input (option 2), and audio absolutely can carry adversarial content — spoken prompt-injection attempts are a real category, making option 3 an overconfident dismissal.

prompt: "If a tool's output always matches its expected schema, its output is trustworthy." True or false?

config.statement: Output that always matches its expected schema is always trustworthy.
config.rubric: A full answer distinguishes schema validity from correctness, not just a flat disagreement.
