hints: Ask what schema validation is actually capable of checking versus what it can't.
Think of a specific example where every field is the right type but the value is still wrong.
explanation: False. Schema validity confirms the output is well-formed — right types, right fields — and says nothing about whether the values in those fields are actually correct, which is the valid-but-wrong failure mode this module covered directly. An off-by-one calculation, a swapped field value, or a wrong-but-allowed category can all match a schema perfectly while being substantively wrong.

prompt: Match each scenario to the edge-case category it best represents.

pairs.left: A user uploads a 0-byte file by mistake
pairs.right: Empty, huge, or malformed input

pairs.left: A résumé written with the family name first, misread by a tool that assumes first-name-first
pairs.right: Input in a language or format you didn't plan for

pairs.left: A function that computes a sum correctly but divides by the wrong count
pairs.right: Output that's technically valid and still wrong

pairs.left: Hidden white text in a document reading instructions to the AI reviewer
pairs.right: Adversarial input aimed at your prompt

hints: Match each scenario to the specific mechanism described in its own lesson.
Two scenarios both involve untested formats, but at different points in the pipeline.
explanation: Each scenario maps directly to one of the module's four failure categories: an accidental empty upload, a valid-but-untested naming convention, a semantically wrong but well-formed calculation, and content-level manipulation smuggled inside legitimate-looking input.

prompt: Put these steps in order for handling a newly-discovered edge case in a shipped tool.

items: Confirm the case reproduces (per the previous module's reproduction discipline)
Decide deliberately whether the right response is to reject, degrade visibly, or ask for clarification
Implement the chosen handling, avoiding silent degradation
Add the case to the short, workflow-embedded edge-case checklist so future features check for it too

hints: Trace the order this module and the previous one built up together — reproduce, decide, implement, then institutionalize.
The last step connects back to this module's own final lesson.
explanation: This connects the previous module's reproduction discipline to this module's handling decision and closes with this module's own final lesson — turning a one-off discovered bug into a permanent, checked-for category rather than a fix that only helps the one case that happened to get reported.

prompt: Sort each response to an oversized document into reject, degrade visibly, or degrade silently.

items.text: Return an error stating the file exceeds the size limit, with no further guidance
Summarize only the first portion of the document, with a clear note that it's a partial summary
Summarize only the first portion of the document with no indication anything was cut
Detect the size up front and offer to summarize the document in sections

hints: The key distinction is visibility to the user, not how much of the document got processed.
Two of the four items produce the exact same visible output — read carefully for what differs.
explanation: The dividing line between the categories is whether the user can tell what happened. A clean rejection and a labeled partial result both leave the user informed, even if the labeled partial result is more useful. An unlabeled partial result is the dangerous case this module specifically warned about — it looks identical to a complete, trustworthy result.

prompt: A tool handles adversarial input well at the message level (system/user separation) but has never been tested against adversarial content hidden inside uploaded documents. Using this module's reasoning, explain why passing the first test doesn't imply passing the second.
hints: Ask whether the two attack types described actually use the same channel or a different one.
One defense is about message-level instructions; the other is about content the tool trusts as data.
explanation: Channel separation and content-level scanning defend against two structurally different attacks — one where instruction-shaped text arrives as a user message, and one where manipulative content is smuggled inside data the tool is supposed to process and trust as legitimate content. A tool that correctly refuses to treat a user message like "ignore your instructions" as a real instruction has solved the first problem, but that defense doesn't touch content buried inside a document field, because the document's content was never claiming to be an instruction to begin with — it's being read as ordinary data the whole time, which is exactly where a hidden instruction can hide undetected.

prompt: A team's edge-case checklist is thorough and well-organized but stored as a standalone document not referenced anywhere in the development process. What does this module predict will happen to it?

options.text: It will be effectively unused, regardless of its content quality, because nothing surfaces it at the point where a relevant decision is being made
It will naturally become the team's most-referenced document over time because it's thorough
It doesn't matter, since edge cases are rare enough not to need active checking

hints: Think about what actually determines whether a document gets used, according to this module's own diagnosis.
explanation: This module's final lesson makes exactly this prediction: content quality doesn't determine usage, location and workflow integration do. A thorough document with no connection to the actual development process is functionally equivalent to no document, however good its content is — thoroughness (option 2) doesn't create usage on its own, and edge cases being common rather than rare (contradicting option 3) is the entire premise of the module.

prompt: Pick any two of this module's four edge-case categories and explain, concretely, why a bug in one of them would NOT necessarily be caught by testing deliberately built for the other. Use a specific example for each.
hints: Pick two categories whose tests would exercise genuinely different parts of the pipeline.
A test built for one category rarely wanders into checking a completely different failure mode by accident.
explanation: There's no single correct pair — this is graded on whether the two chosen categories are genuinely distinguished with concrete examples rather than restated in the abstract. A strong answer might contrast valid-but-wrong output (e.g., an off-by-one calculation that returns a well-typed but incorrect number) with adversarial input (e.g., hidden text in a document manipulating the model's judgment) and explain that a known-answer boundary case would never encounter the hidden-text scenario at all, since it's testing arithmetic correctness on clean input, not scanning for embedded manipulation — the two failure modes live in genuinely different parts of the pipeline and require different, deliberately-targeted tests. A weaker answer treats the categories as interchangeable or just restates their definitions without showing why one wouldn't catch the other.

prompt: A team compares two versions of a code-review tool by having one senior engineer read through ten example reviews from each version and pick which set feels more helpful overall. What's the core limitation of this approach?

options.text: One person's subjective impression of ten examples doesn't check whether either version actually catches more real defects, or the same defects consistently
Ten examples is too few for any evaluation approach to be meaningful
A senior engineer's judgment is inherently unreliable for this kind of comparison

hints: The problem isn't the reviewer's competence or the exact number ten — it's what "feels more helpful" is actually measuring versus what it isn't.
Compare this to the concrete failure from this lesson's opening scenario — what would have caught it?
explanation: "Feels more helpful" is measuring writing style, tone, and general impression — not whether the review actually catches real defects, or catches them consistently across a representative range of code. Ten examples could be enough if they were a fixed, representative set with known correct findings checked against — the actual problem is the lack of a checkable, predetermined outcome, not the raw count. Dismissing the engineer's competence (option 3) misses the point; even the most skilled reviewer can't turn a subjective impression into a measurement of defect-catching accuracy just by being good at their job.

prompt: A team building their first eval set for a receipt-categorizer wants to start with 'whatever receipts we have lying around from testing.' Explain what's likely missing from that starting point, and what you'd add.
hints: Think about what 'whatever we have lying around' is likely to be skewed toward, compared to the tool's real range of use.
Consider both the representativeness gap and the known-answer gap separately.
explanation: Receipts lying around from testing are likely to be whatever the team happened to use during development — probably skewed toward clean, easy, well-formatted examples, and very likely missing a deliberate spread across the tool's real difficulty range (smudged receipts, receipts with multiple totals, unusual vendor formats) and the edge cases from the previous module (an empty upload, a non-receipt file). They're also likely to lack a verified, predetermined correct category for each one, which is what actually makes a case usable for measurement rather than just for a demo. A stronger starting point deliberately samples across difficulty and format, hand-verifies the correct category for each case, and explicitly includes a few edge cases — turning an ad hoc pile into a fixed, checkable set.

prompt: Which of these eval cases is the best candidate for fully automated, exact-match scoring?

options.text: A tool that extracts a due date from an email into a structured field
A tool that writes a two-paragraph explanation of a legal clause
A tool that suggests a friendly, on-brand response to a customer review

hints: Ask which of these three outputs reduces to one specific, comparable correct value versus open-ended free text.
A due date is a specific fact with one correct answer, unlike a written explanation or a suggested response.
explanation: A due date extracted into a structured field has exactly one correct value for a given email, making it a clean candidate for exact-match scoring against a known-correct date. A written explanation and a suggested response are both open-ended free text where many different phrasings could be equally correct or equally good — forcing exact-match scoring onto either would repeat the mistake this lesson's spot-flaw drill just diagnosed.

prompt: Sort each eval case into the scoring approach that fits it best.

items.text: Whether an extracted phone number matches the known-correct number
Whether a generated summary mentions every action item present in the source transcript
Whether a drafted marketing email has the right persuasive tone for the brand
Whether an assigned support category matches the known-correct category from a fixed list
Whether generated code compiles and passes a known-answer test case

hints: Ask whether each item reduces to one specific correct value, a checkable property that doesn't require exact wording, or a genuinely subjective judgment.
Compiling and passing a test is a property that can be checked mechanically, even though the code's exact text can vary.
explanation: Extracted phone numbers and assigned categories both have one specific correct value, making exact-match the right fit. Whether a summary mentions every action item, or whether code compiles and passes a known-answer test, are both checkable properties that don't require the output to match any specific wording — a good fit for automated property checks. Tone and persuasive quality are genuinely subjective judgments no automated check can reliably make, which is exactly the remainder the next lesson's sampled human review is for.

prompt: "If a quality dimension can't be automatically scored, the honest response is to skip evaluating it rather than invent an imperfect proxy metric." True or false?

config.statement: A quality dimension that can't be automatically scored should simply be skipped rather than evaluated any other way.
config.rubric: A full answer names sampled human review as the actual honest alternative, not just disagreeing with skipping it.

hints: The lesson argues against two specific wrong answers — what's the third, correct option?
Compare 'invent a bad proxy' and 'skip entirely' to what the lesson actually recommends.
explanation: False — skipping isn't the honest alternative to a bad proxy metric either. The lesson's actual position is a third option: sampled human review against an explicit rubric, which is smaller in scope than full manual coverage but genuinely measures the real quality dimension, rather than either (a) forcing it into a keyword-checklist proxy that measures something only loosely related to real quality, or (b) abandoning measurement of that dimension entirely, which leaves the tool's subjective quality completely unmonitored and free to degrade unnoticed.

prompt: A team samples 10 headlines for human review, but always pulls the 10 most recently generated ones at the moment someone remembers to check. What's the specific risk with this sampling method?

options.text: It's not representative — 'most recent at whatever moment someone remembers' is driven by convenience and timing, not by deliberately covering the tool's real range of output
10 is too small a sample size for any conclusion at all
Recent outputs are always worse than older ones

hints: The problem identified in the lesson's build-it drill wasn't sample size — it was what determines which examples get selected.
Ask what 'whatever's most recent when someone remembers' is likely to systematically miss.
explanation: The core issue is what determines selection — 'most recent, whenever someone happens to remember' means the sample is shaped by timing and memory rather than by a deliberate plan to cover the tool's real range, similar to the 'whatever's convenient' failure from the eval-set lesson earlier in this module. Ten is a reasonable size for this kind of spot-check per the lesson's own build-it drill (option 2 overstates the size problem), and there's no basis for assuming recent output is systematically worse (option 3) — the risk is about representativeness, not recency itself.

prompt: A team runs their eval harness once a week, regardless of how many changes shipped that week. A regression is found on Friday's run. What's the main cost of this cadence, given everything else about the harness works correctly?

options.text: The regression could have been introduced by any of the week's changes, making it much harder to isolate the actual cause
Weekly runs are too frequent and waste compute resources
The eval set itself must be flawed if it only caught the regression a week later

hints: Think about how many candidate causes exist for a regression found after a whole week of shipped changes, versus one found right after a single change.
The eval set doing its job correctly and the cadence being too infrequent are two separate things — which one is actually at fault here?
explanation: With a week's worth of changes between eval runs, a regression found on Friday could trace back to any change made that week — exactly the localization problem this lesson's diagnosis mechanism describes, a direct parallel to the earlier module's reproduce-and-isolate difficulty when too much time or too many changes separate a bug from its cause. Weekly runs aren't wastefully frequent (option 2 has it backwards — the problem is infrequency, not overuse), and the eval set isn't at fault for catching the regression a week late (option 3) — it did its job the moment it ran; the schedule is what delayed that.

prompt: Put these in the order that best reflects how confident you should be that a given change needs an eval harness run before merging, from most clearly needed to most clearly unnecessary.

items: A direct edit to the prompt template's wording
A change to the logic that retrieves and assembles context for the request
A refactor of an unrelated part of the codebase that happens to touch the same file, with no behavior change
A typo fix in a code comment

hints: Rank based on how directly each change could plausibly affect the model's actual behavior, not on how large the code diff looks.
A large-looking diff (a refactor) with genuinely zero behavior change ranks below a tiny but behavior-relevant one.
explanation: A direct prompt edit is the clearest, most direct trigger. Context-assembly logic is the previous module's 'context' suspect and deserves the same trigger, just one step removed from the prompt itself. A same-file refactor with no actual behavior change is a case where the diff might look large but the risk is genuinely low — still arguably worth a quick check given the ambiguity, but well below the first two. A comment typo fix has zero plausible effect on runtime behavior and is the clearest case where triggering a full eval run would just be friction.

prompt: An eval harness shows a quality metric dropped after a change. The engineer says "the new version looks fine to me though" and merges anyway. What does this module say about that decision?

options.text: It repeats the exact failure mode this module opened with — trusting a personal impression over an actual measurement on a fixed, representative set
It's reasonable, since a single engineer's judgment is generally more reliable than an automated score
It's fine as long as the drop is small

hints: Compare this decision to the very first scenario in this module's first lesson.
The size of the drop isn't really the point here — what's the actual reasoning error?
explanation: This is the module's opening mistake, replayed: a personal impression ("looks fine to me") overriding an actual measurement from a fixed, representative eval set — exactly the "three engineers agreeing it sounds better" scenario the module opened with, which turned out to have missed a tripled real-world failure rate. A single engineer's impression isn't inherently more reliable than a measured score (option 2 gets this backwards), and the size of the drop isn't really the issue (option 3) — the issue is which source of evidence the team chose to trust when they disagreed.

prompt: Design a lightweight, concrete trigger for updating a stale eval set — something that would have caught the three-categories-to-nine-categories gap from this lesson before it grew to two-thirds of the tool's functionality being uncovered. Be specific about what event triggers the update, not just "review periodically."
hints: A trigger tied to a specific, recurring event in the actual development process is stronger than a vague calendar reminder.
Think about what already happens in the team's workflow when a new capability ships — could the eval-set update piggyback on that same moment?
explanation: A concrete, workable trigger: whenever a new category, feature, or capability ships (the same kind of event that would already require updating documentation or the edge-case checklist from the previous module), add at least 2-3 representative eval cases for it as part of that same change's checklist — piggybacking the eval-set update onto a moment that's already happening in the workflow, rather than relying on a separate, easy-to-forget calendar reminder. A secondary, lower-frequency trigger — a quarterly review comparing the eval set's coverage against the tool's current real capability list — catches anything that slipped through the per-feature trigger. A weaker answer just proposes 'review the eval set periodically' without naming a specific event or cadence, which is exactly the vague, easy-to-skip pattern this lesson's scenario already showed doesn't reliably happen on its own.

prompt: A team wants to eval a tool that extracts structured order details (item, quantity, price) from customer emails. What's the best eval-set composition?

options.text: A representative fixed set of real order emails spanning easy and hard cases, each with a hand-verified known-correct extraction
The 500 most recent order emails, unverified, scored by whether extraction 'looks reasonable'
A single, very clean example email, run repeatedly

hints: Ask which option has both real coverage and known-correct answers to check against.
A single repeated example has neither representativeness nor difficulty range.
explanation: A fixed, representative, hand-verified set is exactly what lesson one established a useful eval set needs — known outcomes and real coverage of the tool's actual difficulty range. 500 unverified recent emails scored by 'looks reasonable' has no known-correct answer to check against, repeating the impression-based mistake the module opened with. A single repeated clean example has no representativeness at all and would miss regressions on anything but that one easy case.

prompt: "Since summaries are free text, no part of a summarization eval can be automatically scored." True or false?

config.statement: No part of a summarization eval can ever be automatically scored, since summaries are free text.
config.rubric: A full answer names a specific checkable property, not just a flat disagreement.

hints: The claim overgeneralizes from one specific scoring method's limits to the whole task being unscoreable.
Think of a specific fact-based property inside a summary that IS checkable.
explanation: False — this overgeneralizes from 'exact-match scoring doesn't work on free text' to 'nothing about it is automatable,' which lesson two specifically argued against. Checkable properties like whether every real action item name from the source appears in the summary, or whether the summary avoids introducing any fact not present in the source, can be automated even though the exact wording can't be. The genuinely subjective remainder (tone, overall polish) is what needs sampled human review, not the whole task.

prompt: Match each eval-harness component to the lesson that introduced it.

pairs.left: A fixed, representative, known-answer case set
pairs.right: A handful of real cases beats a vague sense it's fine

pairs.left: Automated property checks for free-text output
pairs.right: Scoring output automatically where you can

pairs.left: A rubric-based sample reviewed by a human on a real cadence
pairs.right: Sampling for human review where you can't

pairs.left: Triggering the harness on prompt, model, context, and parsing changes specifically
pairs.right: Running the harness before every real change

hints: Match based on which specific lesson title introduced each concept.
The order of the pairs follows the module's own lesson sequence.
explanation: Each pairing traces directly to the lesson that introduced it: the fixed case set from lesson one, automated property scoring from lesson two, rubric-based sampling from lesson three, and change-triggered cadence from lesson four — the module's four-lesson arc in order.

prompt: Put these steps in order for building an eval harness for a new AI-powered feature from scratch.

items: Build a fixed, representative case set with known-correct or known-acceptable outcomes
Automate scoring for everything that reduces to a checkable property
Build a rubric-based sampled review process for the genuinely subjective remainder
Wire the harness to run automatically before merging any behavior-relevant change

hints: The dependency chain matters — you can't decide what's automatable before you have known answers to check against.
Wiring into CI only makes sense once scoring is fast enough to run constantly.
explanation: This mirrors the module's own lesson order for a reason — you can't decide what to automatically score (step 2) before you have known-correct outcomes to check against (step 1), the subjective remainder (step 3) is only knowable once you've separated out what's automatable, and wiring the harness into the actual workflow (step 4) only matters once there's something fast enough to run on every relevant change.

prompt: Sort each code or config change into whether it should trigger an automatic eval harness run.

items.text: Editing the wording of the system prompt
Fixing a typo in the README
Changing which fields get retrieved and inserted into the request context
Renaming a private internal variable with no behavior change

hints: Ask whether each change could plausibly shift what the model actually outputs.
A behavior-neutral rename has zero effect on runtime output regardless of how it looks in a diff.
explanation: The dividing line from lesson four is whether a change could plausibly affect actual output behavior. Prompt wording and context-assembly logic both can; documentation and behavior-neutral renames can't, and triggering a full eval run for either would just be friction with no corresponding safety benefit.

prompt: A solo developer with one small AI feature says building a full eval harness — fixed set, automated scoring, sampled review, CI trigger — feels like overkill for their scale. What's a genuinely minimal but real version of this module's advice that would still be worth building?
hints: The core disciplines don't require large scale to apply — think about what stays true even at 5-8 cases instead of 20-30.
explanation: A genuinely minimal version keeps the core structure at a much smaller scale rather than skipping it: 5-8 representative cases (not 20-30) with hand-verified expected outcomes, a short script that checks whatever's mechanically checkable (even a simple substring or keyword check counts), a manual but deliberate spot-check of 2-3 outputs against a short mental rubric before any prompt change ships, and running the whole small script by hand before any change that touches the prompt or model config — the same shape as a full harness, sized down, rather than a different, lesser thing. What matters is preserving the core disciplines (known answers, some automation, some real review, triggered at the right moment) even at a fraction of the scale, not matching a large team's exact scope.

prompt: An eval set was built when a tool supported two languages and has never been updated, though the tool now supports six. What does this module say is the risk?

options.text: The eval set silently stops representing a majority of the tool's real functionality, and regressions in the newer languages could go completely uncaught
Nothing — a fixed eval set is supposed to stay exactly as it was built, forever, by design
The eval set should be entirely rebuilt from scratch every time any feature is added

hints: Distinguish 'fixed as in stable for comparison' from 'fixed as in never touched again.'
explanation: This is exactly the staleness risk lesson five's second half describes — a fixed set is fixed for stable comparison, not fixed in the sense of never needing updates, and letting it silently fall behind real functionality growth leaves whole categories of regression uncaught. 'Fixed forever by design' (option 2) misreads what 'fixed' means in this context. A full rebuild on every single feature addition (option 3) overcorrects — the lesson's actual advice is targeted incremental additions tied to real events, not scrapping the comparable baseline every time.
